patches.old:
- **Alpha (α) cells** (~20% of islet cells): secrete **glucagon**
- **Beta (β) cells** (~70% of islet cells): secrete **insulin** and **amylin**
patches.new:
- **Alpha (α) cells** (roughly 20–40% of islet cells; a larger share in human than in rodent islets): secrete **glucagon**
- **Beta (β) cells** (roughly 50–70% of islet cells; a smaller share in humans): secrete **insulin** and **amylin**
patches.reason: Human islets contain proportionally fewer β cells and more α cells than rodent islets.

patches.old: The spatial organization matters: β cells occupy the core of the islet, surrounded by α and δ cells at the periphery. Blood flows from the β-cell core outward, so insulin bathing the α cells is one mechanism by which high glucose *suppresses* glucagon release
patches.new: The spatial organization matters: in rodent islets, β cells form the core and α and δ cells form an outer mantle, with blood thought to flow from the core outward. Human islets are more intermingled, with many direct α–β cell contacts. In both, insulin and other β-cell products act locally on α cells (paracrine signaling), which is one mechanism by which high glucose *suppresses* glucagon release
patches.reason: The classic core–mantle picture describes rodent islets; human islet architecture is more mixed.

patches.old: PKA phosphorylates and activates **hormone-sensitive lipase (HSL)** and **perilipin**, releasing fatty acids and glycerol from triglycerides.
patches.new: In the standard model, PKA phosphorylates and activates **hormone-sensitive lipase (HSL)** and **perilipin**, releasing fatty acids and glycerol from triglycerides. (In humans, adipocytes express few glucagon receptors and physiological glucagon levels have little direct lipolytic effect; fasting lipolysis is driven mainly by falling insulin and by catecholamines acting through the same cAMP–PKA–HSL pathway.)
patches.reason: Evidence that glucagon has minor direct effects on human adipocytes at physiological levels.

patches.old: | GLUT1 | RBCs, brain, placenta, most cells | Constitutive, high affinity (Km ~1 mM) |
patches.new: | GLUT1 | RBCs, brain, placenta, most cells | Constitutive, high affinity (Km ~1–3 mM) |
patches.reason: Reported GLUT1 Km values range about 1–3 mM (some sources higher).

patches.old: | GLUT3 | Neurons | Very high affinity (Km ~0.1 mM); ensures brain glucose uptake |
patches.new: | GLUT3 | Neurons | Highest affinity of the main isoforms (Km ~1.4 mM); ensures neuronal glucose uptake |
patches.reason: GLUT3's Km is about 1.4 mM, not 0.1 mM.

patches.old: Choice A reverses the roles of insulin and glucagon, which is the most common error students make when confusing the direction of each hormone's effect.
patches.new: Choice A reverses the roles of insulin and glucagon, which is the most common error students make when confusing the direction of each hormone's effect. (This is the standard textbook contrast; in humans, glucagon's direct effect on fat cells is small, and catecholamines plus low insulin drive most fasting lipolysis.)
patches.reason: Keeps the expected answer while noting the human-physiology caveat.

visual.title: Glucose sensing and the fed–fasted switch
visual.alt: Six steps of glucose-stimulated insulin secretion: glucose enters via GLUT2, glucokinase phosphorylates it, ATP/ADP rises, K-ATP channels close and the cell depolarizes, voltage-gated calcium channels open, and insulin with C-peptide is exocytosed. Sulfonylureas close K-ATP channels; diazoxide opens them. Below, insulin acts via a receptor tyrosine kinase, PI3K and Akt to promote storage, while glucagon acts via a Gs-coupled receptor, cAMP and PKA mainly in liver to mobilize glucose and fat.
visual.caption: The insulin-to-glucagon ratio, not either hormone alone, sets whether the liver stores or releases fuel.
